lesson.title: Matrix shape and transpose

steps.headline: A matrix is a table of numbers. Its shape is its rows by its columns, and its transpose flips it.

lead.text: Rows run across and columns run down. A matrix with 2 rows and 3 columns has shape 2 × 3. Entry (i, j) sits in row i and column j.
The transpose Aᵀ turns row i into column i. Entry (i, j) of A becomes entry (j, i) of Aᵀ.
A matrix times a vector pairs each entry of a row with an entry of the vector, one by one. A has 2 rows and 3 columns.

reveal.text: You matched the vector to a row of A. Each row is as long as the matrix has columns, so the vector needs exactly that many entries.

steps.headline: Find the transpose of a 2 × 3 matrix with rows (1, 2, 3) and (4, 5, 6).

workedSteps.text: Row 1 becomes column 1, and row 2 becomes column 2.

steps.headline: Find entry (3, 2) of Aᵀ, where A = $\begin{pmatrix}1&4&-2\\3&0&5\end{pmatrix}$.

workedSteps.text: Transposing swaps the positions. Entry (3, 2) of Aᵀ is entry (2, 3) of A.
Read entry (2, 3) of A. Count rows and columns from 1.

lead.text: The matrix A is $\begin{pmatrix}1&4&-2\\3&0&5\end{pmatrix}$. Transposing turns every row of A into a column.

reveal.text: You counted the rows of A, because those become the columns of Aᵀ. Shape 2 × 3 flips to 3 × 2.

lead.text: A table of sales is the matrix $\begin{pmatrix}1&4&-2\\3&0&5\end{pmatrix}$. Each row is a shop and each column is a day.

lesson.orientation: Read rows and columns, transpose entries and check input dimensions.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A timetable has 4 days across the top and 7 periods down the side. You flip it so that the days run down the side.

intro.promise: By the end you'll read a matrix's shape and flip it with the transpose, finding any entry by its row and column.

recap.keyIdea: A matrix is a table with a shape of rows by columns. Its transpose swaps the two: entry (i, j) moves to position (j, i).

blocks.text: You saw that a matrix with three columns needs a three-entry vector, found entry (3, 2) of Aᵀ, and showed that transposing swaps the row and column counts.

recap.nextHook: A matrix acting on a vector is a map. Next, see how its columns decide where every vector goes.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The 7 periods move from down the side to across the top.

questions.prompt: How many periods run across the top of the flipped timetable?
hints: Which direction do the periods run in the original timetable?
Flipping swaps the across and down directions.
The periods move from the side to the top. How many are there?

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of days. In the flipped timetable they run down the side.

questions.onCorrect: 7. Flipping a table swaps which way each label runs. A matrix transpose does just that.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It has 2 rows and 3 columns, so its shape is 2 × 3.

questions.prompt: What is the shape of the matrix $\begin{pmatrix}5&6&7\\8&9&0\end{pmatrix}$?
hints: Count the rows first, then the columns.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the shape of its transpose. Count rows first, then columns.
That counts all the entries. Shape is the number of rows by the number of columns.

questions.onCorrect: Rows first, then columns: 2 rows and 3 columns make shape 2 × 3.

questions.prompt: A has 2 rows and 3 columns. How many entries must v have for A v to make sense?
hints: Each row of A pairs up with v, entry by entry.
How many entries does one row of A have?
A row is as long as the matrix has columns.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A has three columns, so each row has three entries and v needs three entries.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of rows. Each row has as many entries as there are columns.

questions.onCorrect: Each row of A pairs with v entry by entry, so v needs one entry per column.

acceptedIdeas: Transposing swaps each entry's row and column.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Row i becomes column i, so every entry swaps its row and column.

questions.prompt: Why does entry (2, 3) of A end up at position (3, 2) in Aᵀ?

choices.label: Transposing swaps each entry's row and column.
Transposing reverses the order of all the entries.
Transposing changes the sign of each entry.

hints: Which of the two numbers in the position does the transpose change?

misconceptions.feedback: Reversing everything would also change the row. The transpose keeps each entry and swaps only its position's two numbers.
The entries stay as they are. Only their positions change.

questions.onCorrect: Row i becomes column i, so each entry's row and column numbers swap.

questions.prompt: For A = $\begin{pmatrix}1&4&-2\\3&0&5\end{pmatrix}$, what is entry (3, 2) of Aᵀ? Count from 1.
hints: Swap the two positions.
Entry (3, 2) of Aᵀ comes from entry (2, 3) of A.
Look in the second row and the third column of A.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Entry (3, 2) of Aᵀ is entry (2, 3) of A, which is 5.

misconceptions.feedback: That is entry (2, 2) of A. Swap the two positions as written.
That is entry (1, 2) of A. Swap the positions, then read the row and column.

questions.onCorrect: Swap the positions: entry (3, 2) of Aᵀ is entry (2, 3) of A.

questions.prompt: For A = $\begin{pmatrix}1&4&-2\\3&0&5\end{pmatrix}$, how many columns does Aᵀ have?
hints: Rows of A become columns of Aᵀ.
Count the rows of A.
The number of rows of A is the number of columns of Aᵀ.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A has two rows, so Aᵀ has two columns.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of columns of A. The transpose swaps rows and columns.

questions.onCorrect: A has two rows, and each becomes a column of Aᵀ.

questions.prompt: For the sales table A = $\begin{pmatrix}1&4&-2\\3&0&5\end{pmatrix}$, how many shops are there?
hints: Each row is a shop.
Count the rows.
Rows run across the matrix.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: There are two rows, and each row is a shop.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of days, which are the columns.

questions.onCorrect: Each row is a shop, so the number of rows is the number of shops.

questions.prompt: Let B = $\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\7&3\\4&0\end{pmatrix}$. What is entry (2, 1) of Bᵀ? Count from 1.
hints: Swap the two positions.
Entry (2, 1) of Bᵀ comes from entry (1, 2) of B.
Look in the first row and the second column of B.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: This is the original entry (1, 2), which is −1.

misconceptions.feedback: That is entry (2, 1) of B itself. Swap the positions first.

questions.onCorrect: Swap the positions: entry (2, 1) of Bᵀ is entry (1, 2) of B.

questions.prompt: A has 3 rows and 2 columns. How many columns does Aᵀ have?
hints: Rows and columns swap.
Which count of A becomes the columns of Aᵀ?
The rows of A become the columns of Aᵀ.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The transpose's column count is the original row count: 3.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of columns of A. The transpose swaps rows and columns.

questions.onCorrect: The transpose swaps the counts, so its columns number as many as A's rows.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Entry (2, 3) of Cᵀ is entry (3, 2) of C, which is 4.

questions.prompt: Let C = $\begin{pmatrix}5&8\\6&9\\7&4\end{pmatrix}$. What is entry (2, 3) of Cᵀ? Count from 1.
hints: Swap the two positions.
Entry (2, 3) of Cᵀ comes from entry (3, 2) of C.
Look in the third row and the second column of C.

misconceptions.feedback: That is entry (2, 2) of C. Check the row and column numbers after swapping.
That is entry (1, 2) of C. Check the row and column numbers after swapping.

questions.onCorrect: Swap the positions: entry (2, 3) of Cᵀ is entry (3, 2) of C.
